overview.text: The President of the United States, often called the U.S. President or POTUS, leads the federal executive branch, serves as commander in chief of the armed forces, and is the nation’s head of state. Article II of the Constitution vests executive power in the office and sets a four-year term, selection through electors, and eligibility requirements: natural-born citizenship, at least 35 years of age, and 14 years’ U.S. residence. The president is responsible for carrying out federal laws and may veto legislation, while important powers such as making treaties and appointing officials involve the Senate’s advice and consent. Checks and balances among the executive, legislative, and judicial branches limit the concentration of government power.

key_facts.text: Article II establishes the presidency as the holder of federal executive power and provides for a four-year term.
Voters choose electors who cast votes for president; this process is known as the Electoral College.
The Constitution’s listed eligibility requirements are natural-born citizenship, age 35 or older, and at least 14 years’ residence in the United States.
The president is commander in chief and must take care that federal laws are faithfully executed.
Presidential powers are checked by other branches: for example, Congress can override a veto, and the Senate confirms many presidential nominees.
